title: NTA UGC NET English Full Mock Test #02
subtitle: 100 Questions · 200 Marks · Post-2018 NTA Pattern · Zero Answer Bias (25 A/B/C/D) · Reading Comprehension (Q91-100)

items.title: Mock #02 · Q1
items.stem:
Match the column:
(A) Christopher Marlowe
(B) William Shakespeare
(C) Thomas Kyd
(D) Ben Jonson
(I) The Winter’s Tale
(II) The Jew of Malta
(III) Every Man in his Humour
(IV) Spanish Tragedy
items.explanation: Christopher Marlowe wrote The Jew of Malta (c. 1589–1590, A-II); William Shakespeare wrote The Winter's Tale (c. 1611, B-I); Thomas Kyd wrote The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587–1590, C-IV); and Ben Jonson wrote Every Man in His Humour (1598, D-III).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q2
items.stem:
Which of the following books is by
Margaret Atwood ?
items.explanation: The Edible Woman (1969) is Margaret Atwood's debut novel, centring on Marian McAlpin, a young woman whose rebellion against consumerism and conventional marriage manifests as an inability to eat. The Stone Angel is by Margaret Laurence.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q3
items.stem:
Which of the following are the premises of Postcolonial Criticism?
A. It rejects the claims of universalism made in the canonical Western literature.
B. It foregrounds the questions of cultural difference and diversity as represented in literary texts.
C. It acts on the principles of peaceful co-existence.
D. It celebrates "hybridity" and "Cultural polyvalency".
E. It resists any attempt at homogenization based on race, class and nationality.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A, B, D and E only
items.explanation: As summarized by Peter Barry in Beginning Theory, postcolonial criticism rejects Eurocentric universalism (A), foregrounds cultural difference and diversity (B), celebrates hybridity and cultural polyvalency (D), and resists homogenization based on race, class, and nationality (E).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q4
items.stem: Which of the following poets describes himself as "not an Indian poet but a poet writing a universal language of poetry, of feeling, of love and hate and sex" ?
items.explanation: Arvind Krishna Mehrotra described himself as 'not an Indian poet but a poet writing a universal language of poetry, of feeling, of love and hate and sex,' rejecting narrow nationalist labels for Indian English verse.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q5
items.stem:
Arrange the following plays in their chronological order :
A. The Country Wife
B. Cymbeline
C. The Spanish Tragedy
D. The Rivals

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological order of the plays is: Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587–1590, C); William Shakespeare's Cymbeline (c. 1611, B); William Wycherley's Restoration comedy The Country Wife (1675, A); and Richard Brinsley Sheridan's The Rivals (1775, D).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q6
items.stem:
"It was a bright cold day in April
and
the
clocks
were
striking
thirteen" - is the opening sentence
of
items.explanation: This famous sentence opens George Orwell's dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), immediately establishing an unsettling, regimented totalitarian world as Winston Smith enters Victory Mansions.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q7
items.stem:
Assertion (A) : Deconstructive reading is apolitical.
Reason (R) : Because it focuses exclusively on language, it overlooks the socio-historical context of texts and is hostile to collective political action.
In the context of the two statements, which one of the following is correct ?
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Following the official UGC key, both statements reflect standard materialist and historicist critiques of early American deconstruction (that it is apolitical and focuses on linguistic play over socio-historical context), with option (B) marked as correct.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q8
items.stem: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman was written by Mary Wollstonecraft. Who wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Man?
items.explanation: Thomas Paine famously wrote Rights of Man (1791) in response to Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, defending republicanism and popular revolution. While Mary Wollstonecraft composed A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790), Paine's defense of human rights in the same controversy is the text intended here among the choices.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q9
items.stem:
In the following list, which two journals relate to the field of post-colonial literature?
(a) Kunapipi
(b) Interventions
(c) Daedalus
(d) Clio
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Kunapipi (founded in 1979 by Anna Rutherford) and Interventions: International Journal of Postcolonial Studies (founded in 1998 by Robert J. C. Young) are both prominent academic journals dedicated to postcolonial literature and theory, making (a) and (b) correct.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q10
items.stem: Harold Skimpole is a character in
items.explanation: Harold Skimpole is a character in Charles Dickens's novel Bleak House (1852–1853). Modelled caricaturally on essayist Leigh Hunt, Skimpole is a charming but thoroughly selfish parasite who claims to be a 'mere child' in matters of money and responsibility while living off the generosity of John Jarndyce.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q11
items.stem:
Match the following :
(Poems) — (Poets)
I. "I hear a fly Buzz" — 1. Wallace Stevens
II. "Birches" — 2. Emily Dickinson
III. "Sunday Morning" — 3. Allen Ginsberg
IV. "A Supermarket in California" — 4. Robert Frost
The correct combination according to the code is :
Codes : I II III IV
items.explanation: 'I heard a Fly buzz - when I died' is by Emily Dickinson (I-2), 'Birches' is by Robert Frost (II-4), 'Sunday Morning' is by Wallace Stevens (III-1), and 'A Supermarket in California' is by Allen Ginsberg (IV-3).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q12
items.stem:
Early in Evelyn Waugh's A Handful of Dust, while Tony and his young son, John Andrew,
walk to the church, John tells his father a story he has heard from the stable manager, Ben
about a mule "who had drunk his company's rum ration" in the First World War and
subsequently died.  What is the mule named ?
items.explanation: In Chapter 2 of Evelyn Waugh's novel A Handful of Dust (1934), young John Andrew Last tells his father Tony a story he heard from the groom Ben about a First World War army mule named Peppermint who drank his company's rum ration and died.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q13
items.stem:
Which two of the following are fallacious evaluations of poetry according to Matthew Arnold's "The Study of Poetry"?
A. contextual estimate
B. personal estimate
C. comparative estimate
D. historic estimate
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In 'The Study of Poetry' (1880), Matthew Arnold warns critics against two fallacious modes of judging poetry—the 'historic estimate' (D) and the 'personal estimate' (B)—which obscure the 'real estimate.'

items.title: Mock #02 · Q14
items.stem: Who coined the phrase "The Two Nations" to describe the disparity in Britain between the rich and the poor ?
items.explanation: British statesman and novelist Benjamin Disraeli coined the phrase in his Condition-of-England novel Sybil, or The Two Nations (1845), describing industrial Britain as divided into two alienated nations—'the Rich and the Poor'—between whom there is no sympathy orshared understanding.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q15
items.stem:
Arrange the following works chronologically:
A. The Heart of Hindustan
B. Occasional Speeches and Writings
C. Eastern Religions and Western Thought
D. Dhammapada
E. The Principal Upanishads
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: These philosophical works by Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan appeared in the following chronological sequence: *The Heart of Hindustan* (A, 1932), *Eastern Religions and Western Thought* (C, 1939), *The Dhammapada* (D, 1950), *The Principal Upanishads* (E, 1953), and *Occasional Speeches and Writings* (B, 1956).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q16
items.stem: John Dryden in his heroic tragedy All for Love takes the story of Shakespeare's
items.explanation: John Dryden's blank-verse tragedy All for Love; or, The World Well Lost (1677) retells the final hours of Mark Antony and Cleopatra, adapting the story of William Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra to conform strictly to the neoclassical unities of time, place, and action.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q17
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labeled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R

Assertion A: Aphorism is a concise expression of doctrine conveyed in a pithy and memorable statement.

Reason R: The term 'aphoria' is gradually applied to any statement generally accepted as true, so that tis now roughly synonymous with maxim,
Inthe light of the above statements, choose the mast appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A,
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
A is correct but Ris not corect
Aisnnot corect but R is corect
items.explanation: An aphorism is a concise, memorable expression of principle or doctrine (Assertion A is correct), and the term has historically broadened to apply to any widely acknowledged truth, making it virtually synonymous with a maxim (Reason R is correct and provides the linguistic justification for A).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q18
items.stem: Who has written The Myth of Sisyphus ?
items.explanation: Albert Camus wrote the philosophical essay The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), in which he articulated his philosophy of the Absurd through the mythological figure of Sisyphus endlessly pushing his boulder up the hill.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q19
items.stem: Which of the following is true about Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot? (A) It illustrates vanity of human kind. (B) It has uncompromising views on humanitarian communism. (C) It projects self-deception, striving to disguise failure. (D) It is a static representation without structure or development. (E) Its incoherent dialogue suggests despair of a society. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953) is a seminal absurdist play that replaces conventional linear dramatic progression with a circular, static structure where nothing happens [(D)], utilizing disjointed and repetitive dialogue to mirror the post-war existential despair of modern civilization [(E)].

items.title: Mock #02 · Q20
items.stem: Who among the following stated that "true philosopher and the true poet are one, and a beauty, which is truth, and a truth, which is beauty, is the aim of both?"
items.explanation: American Transcendentalist Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote in Chapter VI ('Idealism') of his foundational essay Nature (1836): 'The true philosopher and the true poet are one, and a beauty, which is truth, and a truth, which is beauty, is the aim of both.'

items.title: Mock #02 · Q21
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I
A. Emily Dickinson
B. Kath Walker
C. Judith Wright
D. Yusef Komunyakaa

List II
I. Woman to Man
II. Banking Potatoes
III. Because I could not stop for Death
IV. We Are Going

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Emily Dickinson wrote 'Because I could not stop for Death' (A-III), Aboriginal Australian poet Kath Walker (Oodgeroo Noonuccal) wrote We Are Going (1964, B-IV), Australian poet Judith Wright wrote Woman to Man (1949, C-I), and African American poet Yusef Komunyakaa wrote 'Banking Potatoes' (D-II).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q22
items.stem:
A poet once referred to an old man as “A tattered coat upon a stick”.  That is an example of
__________.
items.explanation: In 'Sailing to Byzantium' (1928), W. B. Yeats writes: 'An aged man is but a paltry thing, / A tattered coat upon a stick', which is a direct metaphorical comparison equating the withered mortal body to a ragged coat hanging on a scarecrow's stick.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q23
items.stem:
Which of these following statements are true about Pidgin and Creole?
(A) Pidgin begins as Creole and eventually becomes the first language of a speech community
(B) Creole begins as Pidgin and eventually becomes the first language of a speech community
(C) Pidgin is simple but a rule governed language developed for communication whereas Creole is free from grammatical rules
(D) Pidgin and Creole evolve successively out of a situation where speakers of mutually unintelligible languages develop a shared language for communication (often based on one of those languages)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: A creole grows out of a pidgin once children learn it as a first language. Both arise when speakers of different languages need a shared tongue.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q24
items.stem: Samuel Pepys began his diary on __________.
items.explanation: Samuel Pepys began keeping his famous private diary on 1 January 1660 (New Year's Day 1660), recording significant historical events of Restoration England including the Great Plague and the Great Fire of London.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q25
items.stem:
Arrange the correct chronological sequence in which the following texts were published:
A. Two Virgins
B. The Painter of Signs
C. Shadow from Ladakh
D. A Bend in the Ganges
E. To Whom She Will
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological publication sequence of these Indian English novels is: Ruth Prawer Jhabvala's To Whom She Will (1955, E), Manohar Malgonkar's A Bend in the Ganges (1964, D), Bhabani Bhattacharya's Shadow from Ladakh (1966, C), Kamala Markandaya's Two Virgins (1973, A), and R.K. Narayan's The Painter of Signs (1976, B), giving E, D, C, A, B.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q26
items.stem: Identify the individual who is a nihilist from the following :
options: Pechorin in A ero of Our Times
items.explanation: In Ivan Turgenev's novel Fathers and Sons (1862), the medical student Yevgeny Bazarov is the quintessential embodiment of Russian 1860s nihilism, repudiating all traditional authority, faith, family sentiments, and Romantic aesthetics in favor of pure natural science.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q27
items.stem:
Given below are two statements—one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : Instances of beliefs triggering action are present in social life and may give rise to problems in determining 'causality'.
Reason (R) : Beliefs may not be accompanied by or give rise to logically appropriate actions, and actions may occur which are consistent with motivations and intentions, but they often, if not usually, also have unanticipated outcomes.
In the light of the above two statements choose the correct option :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Beliefs and actions do not link neatly and have unexpected results, which is why causality is hard to fix.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q28
items.stem:
"No man is truly great, who is great only
in his lifetime. The test of greatness is
the page of history. Nothing can be said
to be great that has a distinct limit, or
that borders on something evidently
greater than itself. Besides, what is short-
lived and pampered into mere notoriety,
is of a gross and vulgar quality in itself."

This passage describing the quality of
greatness is taken from
options: Essay of Dramatic Poesy by John Dryden
Preface to Shakespeare by Samuel Johnson
The Indian Jugglers" by William Hazlitt
items.explanation: This passage on the nature of enduring greatness comes from William Hazlitt's essay "The Indian Jugglers," published in Table-Talk (1821), where he contrasts mechanical skill and fleeting notoriety with true intellectual and artistic genius.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q29
items.stem:
Pick out two Austen heroines from the following list who are right-minded but neglected in
the beginning but gradually are acknowledged to be correct by characters who have previously
looked down on them.
(a)
Elizabeth Bennet
(b)
Fanny Price
(c)
Emma Woodhouse
(d)
Anne Elliot
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Fanny Price in Mansfield Park (1814) and Anne Elliot in Persuasion (1817) are Jane Austen's two quiet, dutiful heroines who are initially overlooked, patronized, or neglected by their vain families, only to be vindicated as morally steadfast and right-minded by the end.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q30
items.stem: ____ the very word is like a bell To toll me back from thee to my sole self ! Which word ?
items.explanation: These lines open the eighth and final stanza of John Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale' (1819). Echoing the word 'forlorn' from the end of Stanza 7 ('perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn'), the word acts like a tolling bell that pulls the speaker back from imaginative transport to his solitary self.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q31
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Author)
A. Nigel Dennis
B. George Orwell
C. Mark Schorer
D. Friedrich Nietzsche

List II (Work)
I. "Technique as Discovery"
II. The Gay Science
III. Cards of Identity
IV. Down and Out in Paris and London

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Nigel Dennis wrote the satirical novel Cards of Identity (1955, A-III); George Orwell authored the memoir Down and Out in Paris and London (1933, B-IV); Mark Schorer wrote the influential critical essay 'Technique as Discovery' (1948, C-I); and Friedrich Nietzsche authored The Gay Science (1882, D-II).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q32
items.stem:
List – I (Text)
A. Kena, Isa, Katha and Mundaka Upanishads (1830s)
B. Ramayana (1870-5)
C. Mahabharata (7 vols 1895)
D. The Bhagvet Geeta (1785)
List – II (Translated by)
I. Ralph T.H. Griffith
II. Manmatha Nath Dutt
III. Charles Wilkins
IV. Ram Mohan Roy
items.explanation: Raja Ram Mohan Roy published English translations of the major Upanishads in the 1810s–1830s (A-IV); Ralph T.H. Griffith published his complete English verse translation of the Ramayana between 1870 and 1874 (B-I); Manmatha Nath Dutt translated the Mahabharata into English prose in seven volumes in the 1890s (C-II); and Charles Wilkins produced the first direct English translation of The Bhagvat-Geeta in 1785 (D-III).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q33
items.stem:
Identify the poems termed as "pastoral elegies" :
A. Lycidas
B. In Memory of W.B. Yeats
C. Adonais
D. Thyrsis
E. In Memoriam
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: John Milton's 'Lycidas' (1637), P. B. Shelley's Adonais (1821), and Matthew Arnold's 'Thyrsis' (1866) are classic English pastoral elegies (A, C and D only), unlike W. H. Auden's modernist elegy 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats' or Tennyson's In Memoriam.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q34
items.stem:
Listed below are the titles of some influential books by Frank Kermode. Identify which one
of the titles that does NOT belong to the set.
options: The Great Code : The Bible and Literature
items.explanation: The Great Code: The Bible and Literature (1982) was written by Canadian myth and archetype critic Northrop Frye, whereas The Sense of an Ending (1967), The Genesis of Secrecy (1979), and the memoir Not Entitled (1995) are major works by Frank Kermode.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q35
items.stem:
Arrange the following stages in a
sequence in which all Shakespearean
tragedies are structured. Use the
code given below :

I.
Denouement

II.
Conflict

III.
Exposition

IV. Climax

Code
items.explanation: Following Gustav Freytag's classical dramatic pyramid, a Shakespearean tragedy progresses sequentially from Exposition (III), through rising Conflict (II), to the turning point or Climax (IV), and concludes with the catastrophe or Denouement (I).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q36
items.stem: The poetic line “’Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all” appears in
options: S.T. Coleridge’s “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner”
Shakespeare’s “Let Me Not to the Marriage of True Minds”
items.explanation: This famous philosophical consolation occurs in Section 27 of Alfred, Lord Tennyson's great Victorian elegy In Memoriam A.H.H. (1850), written over seventeen years in grief for his Cambridge friend Arthur Henry Hallam.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q37
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Human bodies, like those of other living organisms, are only 'sexed' from a particular narrow perspective.
Statement II: Most of the reproductions that we undertake in our lifetimes has nothing to do with 'sex.'
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
items.explanation: Both Statement I and Statement II are true: in gender and queer theory (as discussed in critiques of biological determinism), human bodies are categorized as 'sexed' only from a narrow reproductive perspective, and most cellular, social, and cultural reproduction in human life has nothing to do with biological sex.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q38
items.stem:
A literary researcher now faced with choosing between a print text and its digital
counterpart chooses the latter mostly to :
options: facilitate the consultation of an exhaustive bibliography
avoid the expense of buying books
enhance his/her understanding of textual variants, if any, between the two media
look for specific words and phrases and lines
items.explanation: In modern literary research, scholars consult digital editions and digitized corpora primarily for computational text-searchability—enabling instantaneous concordance searches for specific terms, recurring collocations, lexical variations, and textual patterns.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q39
items.stem:
Which of the following does Urvashi Butalia's The Other Side of Silence primarily seek to do?
A. To understand the Partition as something more than a political divide
B. To foreground a personal history of the Partition
C. To foreground the Partition as an event more tragic than the Holocaust
D. To find and unite families separated at the Partition
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Urvashi Butalia's oral history The Other Side of Silence: Voices from the Partition of India (1998) moves beyond high-political constitutional history (A) to recover the silenced personal testimonies of women, children, and marginalized survivors (B).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q40
items.stem: "I am a sick man... I am a spiteful man. I am an unattractive man. I think my liver is diseased." These are the opening lines of:
options: Gabriel Garcia Marquez's Love in the Time of Cholera
Daniel Defoe's A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: These famously cynical and self-lacerating lines open Fyodor Dostoevsky's groundbreaking existentialist novella Notes from Underground (1864), spoken by the unnamed Underground Man in Saint Petersburg.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q41
items.stem:
William Blake has a rare elan to provide telling images in arresting phrases. Match the phrases
with the poems they belong to :
(a)
"mind forg'd manacles"
(i)
"The Tyger"
(b)
"eternal winter"
(ii)
"The Sick Rose"
(c)
"fearful symmetry"
(iii)
"London"
(d)
"crimson joy"
(iv)
"Holy Thursday"
Code :
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: William Blake's famous phrases from Songs of Experience (1794) match his poems as follows: (a) 'mind-forg'd manacles' in 'London' (iii); (b) 'eternal winter' in 'Holy Thursday' (iv); (c) 'fearful symmetry' in 'The Tyger' (i); and (d) 'crimson joy' in 'The Sick Rose' (ii).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q42
items.meta: Unit VI: English in India: History, Evolution & Futures
items.stem: Who was the writer of A Sketch of Anglo-Indian Literature?
items.explanation: Edward Farley Oaten (E. F. Oaten) authored A Sketch of Anglo-Indian Literature (1908), which grew out of his Cambridge Le Bas Prize essay and represents the first systematic historical survey of British-Indian colonial writing.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q43
items.stem:
Which of the following works of Feminist criticism have been written by Toril Moi?
A. French Feminist Thought: A Reader
B. Feminisms: A Reader
C. Feminist Literary Criticism
D. Sexual/Textual Politics
E. What is a Woman?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Norwegian feminist theorist Toril Moi edited French Feminist Thought: A Reader (1987, A) and authored Sexual/Textual Politics: Feminist Literary Theory (1985, D) and What Is a Woman? And Other Essays (1999, E).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q44
items.stem:
"But deeds, and language, such as men
do use;

And persons, such as comedy would
choose,

When she would show an image of the
time,

and sport with human follies, not with
crime."

In the above lines Jonson

I.
Opposes the artificiality of the
romantic tragic-comedy.

II.
Initiates the use of realism.

III.
Considers analysis of moral short
comings more important

IV.
Encourages the use of farce with
melodrama.

Find out the correct combination
according to the code
options: I, II and IV are correct
I, II and III are correct
I, III and IV are correct
II, III and IV are correct
items.explanation: In the Prologue to Every Man in His Humour (added for the 1616 Folio), Ben Jonson outlines his neoclassical theory of comedy, rejecting romantic improbabilities (I), advocating realistic speech and characters (II), and satirizing everyday human follies rather than crimes (III).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q45
items.stem: Arrange the following forms in the order in which they appeared. Use the code given below : I. commedia dell'arte II. confessional poetry III. agitprop IV. picaresque novel The correct combination is : Code
items.explanation: Commedia dell'arte (I) emerged in early 16th-century Italy, closely followed by the Spanish picaresque novel (IV) with Lazarillo de Tormes (1554). Agitprop theatre (III) arose in post-1917 Soviet Russia, and Confessional poetry (II) developed in the late 1950s in the United States with Robert Lowell's Life Studies (1959).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q46
items.stem: Identify the roup below which is known as the “Sons of Ben”.
options: Noel Coward, E.G. Craig, William Macready, Matheson, Lang
William Cartwright, Richard Corbett, Thomas Randolph
John Dryden, the Earl of Rochester, Samuel Butler
William Holman Hunt, John E. Millais, D.G. Rossetti, William Morris
items.explanation: The 'Sons of Ben' (or the 'Tribe of Ben') were early seventeenth-century Cavalier lyricists and dramatists who gathered around Ben Jonson at London taverns, including William Cartwright, Richard Corbett, Thomas Randolph, and Robert Herrick.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q47
items.stem:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements and choose the correct answer using the code given below :
Assertion (A) : Gender studies do not see an urgent need to help us navigate the various pitfalls of racism, ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, and plain ignorance that flow from using “culture” as an explanatory tool.
Reason (R) : Issues relating to women’s rights, gender roles, sexuality and family obligations are centrally implicated in the so-called clash of civilizations between Christianity or Secularism, and Islam.
items.explanation: Assertion (A) claims gender studies see no urgent need, while (R) shows gender issues are central to cultural clashes, which argues the opposite. So (R) does not follow from (A).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q48
items.stem:
One of the following statements about the eponymous saint of Dryden's "Song for St. Cecilia's
Day" is incorrect.  Identify that statement
options: Cecilia was a Roman lady, an early Christian martyr
Cecilia's festival is celebrated on 22 November in England
Cecilia was an Armenian devotee of the Christian faith
Cecilia was a patroness of music who was fabled to have invented the organ
items.explanation: Saint Cecilia, the patron saint of music celebrated in John Dryden's ode 'A Song for St. Cecilia's Day' (1687) on her feast day of 22 November, was a noble Roman Christian martyr of the second or third century, not an Armenian devotee.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q49
items.stem:
Which of these are true about New Historicism?

A. New Historicists do not use thick descriptions for the examination of cultural production

B. Literary works are not autonomous and timeless

C. History is always narrated. History is a matter of interpretation.

D. All historical analysis is objective

E. History is neither progressive nor linear

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Statements C and E are core tenets of New Historicism: history is viewed as a narrated, interpretive construct rather than an objective reality, and historical change is understood as non-linear and non-teleological. Statement A is false because New Historicists famously employ Clifford Geertz's 'thick descriptions,' while Statement D is false because they reject the belief in objective historical analysis.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q50
items.stem: Who among the following represents the global spread of English diagrammatically as three concentric circles?
items.explanation: Indian-American linguist Braj B. Kachru formulated the 'Three Concentric Circles' model of World Englishes in 1985, categorizing varieties into the Inner Circle, the Outer Circle, and the Expanding Circle.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q51
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Author)
A. Ann Radcliffe
B. Oliver Goldsmith
C. A. C. Swinburne
D. Lord Byron

List II (Work)
I. The Deserted Village
II. The Romance of the Forest
III. The Vision of Judgement
IV. The Sisters

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A - III, B - II, C - I, D - IV
A - III, B - IV, C - I, D - II
A - II, B - I, C - IV, D - III
A - II, B - IV, C - III, D - I
items.explanation: Ann Radcliffe authored the Gothic romance The Romance of the Forest (1791, A-II); Oliver Goldsmith composed the pastoral poem The Deserted Village (1770, B-I); A.C. Swinburne published the verse tragedy The Sisters (1892, C-IV); and Lord Byron wrote the satirical poem The Vision of Judgement (1822, D-III).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q52
items.stem:
Which chilling novel of surveillance and entrapment had the alternative title Things as
They Are ?
items.explanation: William Godwin's radical political thriller Caleb Williams (1794), which portrays the relentless pursuit and surveillance of the servant Caleb after he uncovers his aristocratic master Falkland's secret murder, was originally published under the title Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of Caleb Williams.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q53
items.stem:
Which of the following denote the three phases of literary feminism according to Elaine Showalter?
A. Feminine
B. Gynic
C. Womanish
D. Feminist
E. Female
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: In A Literature of Their Own (1977), Elaine Showalter divides the evolution of women's writing into three historical phases: the Feminine (1840–1880), the Feminist (1880–1920), and the Female (1920–present), corresponding to A, D and E only.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q54
items.stem:
Writing his ost influential play, August Strindberg called it “My ost beloved drama, the
child of y reatest suffering.” The play is :
items.explanation: Swedish dramatist August Strindberg designated A Dream Play (Ett drömspel, 1901) as 'my most beloved drama, the child of my greatest suffering', pioneering an expressionistic, dreamlike dramaturgy where time and space dissolve.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q55
items.stem: Which of the following arrangements is in the correct chronological sequence ?
options: Native Son by Richard Wright - Invisible Man by Ralph Ellison - Their Eyes Were Watching God by Zora Neil Hurston - Another Country by James Baldwin
Their Eyes Were Watching God by Zora Neil Hurston - Another Country by James Baldwin - Native Son by Richard Wright - Invisible Man by Ralph Ellison
Invisible Man by Ralph Ellison - Native Son by Richard Wright - Another Country by James Baldwin - Their Eyes Were Watching God by Zora Neil Hurston
Their Eyes Were Watching God by Zora Neil Hurston - Native Son by Richard Wright - Invisible Man by Ralph Ellison - Another Country by James Baldwin
items.explanation: The correct chronological order of these African American novels is: Zora Neale Hurston's Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), Richard Wright's Native Son (1940), Ralph Ellison's Invisible Man (1952), and James Baldwin's Another Country (1962).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q56
items.stem:
James Thomson's long poem, The Seasons, revised and expanded all his life, began in the
first instance as a poem entitled
items.explanation: Scottish poet James Thomson's blank-verse nature poem The Seasons (completed in 1730) began with the publication of 'Winter' in 1726, followed by 'Summer' (1727), 'Spring' (1728), and 'Autumn' (1730).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q57
items.stem:
Given below are two statements
Statement I: New Historicism stipulates that teleological connotations of history have to be eschewed.
Statement II: New Historicism neither denies nor accepts totalizing explanations of historical events.
In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
items.explanation: Influenced by Michel Foucault, New Historicism rejects linear, teleological grand narratives of history (Statement I is true); consequently, it explicitly rejects—rather than remaining neutral toward—totalizing explanations of historical events (Statement II is false).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q58
items.stem: Which of the following sets would you call the poets of the Movement ?
options: W.H. Auden, Cecil Day Lewis, Stephen Spender
Elizabeth Jennings, Philip Larkin, John Wain
T.S. Eliot, Richard Aldington, Ezra Pound
Alan Brownjohn, C.H. Sisson, Anthony Thwaite
items.explanation: The Movement was a 1950s British group of anti-romantic, restrained poets anthologized in Robert Conquest's New Lines (1956), featuring Elizabeth Jennings, Philip Larkin, John Wain, Kingsley Amis, and Donald Davie.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q59
items.stem: Which of the following is true about Arthur Miller's plays? (A) After the Fall is a semi-autobiographical play. (B) Incident of Vichy deals with Nazi prosecution of the Jews. (C) The Price anticipates economic crash. (D) The Creation of the World is not a serio-comic re-writing of the story of Jesus. (E) The Crucible uses a specific setting to consider the responsibilities of the artist. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Arthur Miller's After the Fall (1964) is an intensely reflective semi-autobiographical drama dramatizing his marriage to Marilyn Monroe and his confrontation with the Red Scare (A), while Incident at Vichy (1964) confronts the Nazi detention, interrogation, and racial persecution of Jews in occupied France (B).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q60
items.stem: How often did Richard Steele's Tatler appear every week and how many issues of Tatler in total were published?
items.explanation: Founded by Richard Steele under the pseudonym Isaac Bickerstaff, Esq., the periodical The Tatler was published three times a week (on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays) from April 12, 1709 to January 2, 1711, running for a total of 271 issues.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q61
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:
List I (Concept/Field):
A. Anthropology
B. Postmodern Geography
C. Diaspora Space
D. Dasein

List II (Thinker):
I. Edward Soja
II. Martin Heidegger
III. Claude Lévi-Strauss
IV. Avtar Brah

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Structural Anthropology is associated with Claude Lévi-Strauss (A-III), Postmodern Geographies (1989) with spatial theorist Edward Soja (B-I), 'Diaspora Space' with sociologist Avtar Brah in Cartographies of Diaspora (1996, C-IV), and 'Dasein' with existential phenomenologist Martin Heidegger (D-II).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q62
items.stem: Who is the author of French novel, Le Journal de Mademoiselle d’Arvers ?
items.explanation: Toru Dutt wrote Le Journal de Mademoiselle d'Arvers, published posthumously in Paris in 1879. It was the first novel in the French language written by an Indian author.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q63
items.stem:
Which two of the following are works by Gustave Flaubert?
A. The Temptation of Saint Anthony
B. Old Goriot
C. Therese Raquin
D. Sentimental Education
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: French realist master Gustave Flaubert authored Sentimental Education (L'Éducation sentimentale, 1869, D) and The Temptation of Saint Anthony (La Tentation de saint Antoine, 1874, A), whereas Old Goriot is by Honoré de Balzac and Thérèse Raquin by Émile Zola.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q64
items.stem:
What 19th-century philosophical term of Russian origin did Friedrich Nietzsche use to describe the disintegration of
traditional morality in western society?
items.explanation: Popularized in Russia by Ivan Turgenev's Fathers and Sons (1862), the term 'nihilism' (from Latin nihil, 'nothing') was adopted by Friedrich Nietzsche to diagnose the collapse of traditional Christian morality and metaphysical values in Western modernity.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q65
items.stem:
Arrange in the chronological order of publication :
(A) The Unfinished Man
(B) Gitanjali
(C) Jejuri
(D) The Sceptred Flute
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Gitanjali (1910), The Sceptred Flute (1943), Jejuri (1974), The Unfinished Man (1976). Marked doubtful since Jejuri and The Unfinished Man are close in date.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q66
items.stem: Teach me half the gladness That thy brain must know, Such harmonious madness From my lips would flow The world should listen then, as I am listening now. Whose lines are these ? To whom are they addressed ?
items.explanation: This is the final stanza of Percy Bysshe Shelley's ode 'To a Skylark' (1820). Addressing the unseen bird soaring in the sky, the poet wishes to learn half its unalloyed joy so that 'harmonious madness' might pour from his own poetic voice.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q67
items.stem:
The salient tendencies of Hellenistic Philosophy are:
A. Cynicism
B. Epicureanism
C. Stoicism
D. Surrealism
E. Expressionism
items.explanation: Hellenistic philosophy (spanning from the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE to the rise of Rome) was defined by Cynicism, Epicureanism, and Stoicism (A, B, and C). Surrealism and Expressionism, by contrast, are modernist aesthetic movements of the 20th century.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q68
items.stem: Little Nell is a character in Dickens's
items.explanation: Little Nell (Nell Trent) is the virtuous, long-suffering young heroine of Charles Dickens's novel The Old Curiosity Shop (1840–1841), whose pathetic death deeply moved Victorian readers.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q69
items.stem:
Match List - I with List - II.
List - I | List - II
(A) Metonymy | (I) Tell me not, Sweet, I am unkind
(B) Paradox | (II) Busy old fool, unruly Sun
(C) Personification | (III) I enjoy reading Shakespeare
(D) Metaphor | (IV) The river snakes its way through the mountains
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: 'I enjoy reading Shakespeare' uses the author's name for his works (metonymy); 'Tell me not, Sweet, I am unkind' is a paradox; 'Busy old fool, unruly Sun' personifies the sun; 'the river snakes' is a metaphor. (Key mildly doubtful: options 2 and 4 swap C and D.)

items.title: Mock #02 · Q70
items.stem: New Science is a work associated with _______
items.explanation: Italian political philosopher and rhetorician Giambattista Vico authored The New Science (Scienza Nuova, 1725), a foundational work in the philosophy of history, myth, and cultural anthropology.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q71
items.stem:
Which two principal kinds of melancholy are proposed by Robert Burton in Volume III of Anatomy of Melancholy?
(a) 'Love'
(b) 'Religious'
(c) 'Morbid'
(d) 'Psychic'
The correct option is:
items.explanation: In the Third Partition (Volume III) of his encyclopedic work The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), Robert Burton examines two principal species of melancholy: Love Melancholy (a) and Religious Melancholy (b).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q72
items.stem: “He’s not the brightest man in the world” is an example of :
items.explanation: The phrase 'He's not the brightest man in the world' employs litotes, using a negative statement to convey an ironic understatement that politely or humorously implies he is foolish or unintelligent.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q73
items.stem:
Arrange the following in ascending order in terms of size :
1. epic
2. epigram
3. stanza
4. sonnet
items.explanation: Arranged in ascending order of length (from shortest to longest), the sequence is: epigram (typically a 2-to-4-line witty statement), stanza (a grouped unit of verse lines), sonnet (a 14-line lyric poem), and epic (a book-length narrative poem).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q74
items.stem:
Two cantos from the seventh book of The Faerie Queene appeared posthumously. They
are known as
items.explanation: The 'Two Cantos of Mutabilitie' (Cantos 6 and 7, along with two stanzas of Canto 8 of an unfinished seventh book) were first published posthumously in the 1609 folio edition of Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q75
items.stem:
Who among the following were Poet Laureates of England?
(A) Alfred Austin
(B) Robert Bridges
(C) Watts-Dunton
(D) Oscar Wilde
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: Alfred Austin (Poet Laureate 1896–1913, A) and Robert Bridges (Poet Laureate 1913–1930, B) were Poets Laureate of England, whereas Theodore Watts-Dunton (C) and Oscar Wilde (D) never held the post; because the printed options omitted '(A) and (B) only,' NTA awarded marks for this question.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q76
items.stem: Lady Dedlock is a character in Dickens’s
items.explanation: Lady Honoria Dedlock is the aristocratic protagonist of Charles Dickens's Bleak House (1852–1853), whose concealed romance with Captain Hawdon and illegitimate daughter Esther Summerson form the novel's central mystery.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q77
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. “Liberty of the Press”
B. “The Vision of Mirza: An Oriental Allegory”
C. “On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth”
D. “Mental Slavery of Modern Workmen”
I. Thomas de Quincey
II. John Ruskin
III. John Milton
IV. Joseph Addison
items.explanation: These prose writings match their authors: John Milton argued for freedom of the press in *Areopagitica* (A-III, 1644), Joseph Addison published 'The Vision of Mirza' in *The Spectator* (B-IV, 1711), Thomas De Quincey wrote 'On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth' (C-I, 1823), and John Ruskin critiqued dehumanizing industrial labor in 'The Nature of Gothic' / 'The Mental Slavery of Modern Workmen' (D-II, 1853).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q78
items.stem: “Politics and the English Language” is an essay by :
items.explanation: George Orwell published his influential critical essay 'Politics and the English Language' in April 1946 in Horizon, critiquing ugly, vague, and dishonest political prose and outlining six rules for clarity in writing.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q79
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their appearance in the English Literary Scene :
(A) Art for Art’s sake
(B) Epistolary Novel
(C) Metaphysical Poetry
(D) Epic Theatre
(E) Stream of Consciousness Technique
items.explanation: The chronological order of appearance in English literary history is Metaphysical Poetry (early 17th century), the Epistolary Novel (mid-18th century), Art for Art's sake (late 19th century Aestheticism), the Stream of Consciousness Technique (early 20th-century modernism), and Epic Theatre (Bertolt Brecht, 1920s–1930s).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q80
items.stem: Of the five conditions of the Sublime, according to Longinus, the most important condition is:
items.explanation: In his classical treatise On the Sublime (Peri Hypsous), Longinus identifies five sources of sublimity in literature. He states that the first and most important condition is 'a lofty cast of mind'—the innate capacity to form grand conceptions and elevated thoughts.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q81
items.stem:
Match the following correctly :
List – I
(I) Mulk Raj Anand
(II) Raja Rao
(III) Prem Chand
(IV) Girish Karnad

List – II
(1) Premashram
(2) The Cat and Shakespeare
(3) Coolie
(4) Nagamandala

Codes : (I) (II) (III) (IV)
items.explanation: Mulk Raj Anand wrote Coolie (3), Raja Rao wrote The Cat and Shakespeare (2), Munshi Premchand wrote Premashram (1), and Girish Karnad wrote the play Nagamandala (4).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q82
items.stem: In poems like "The Altar" and "Easter Wings" ________ exploits _______
items.explanation: In his devotional collection The Temple (1633), Metaphysical poet George Herbert famously used pattern poetry (carmina figurata) in 'The Altar' and 'Easter-Wings,' arranging line lengths and typographic space on the page so that the printed poems visually resemble an altar and pairs of wings.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q83
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order :
1. Mary Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Women
2. Lyrical Ballads
3. French Revolution
4. Percy's Reliques of Ancient English Poetry
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence is Thomas Percy's Reliques of Ancient English Poetry (1765), the outbreak of the French Revolution (1789), Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), and Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads (1798), giving 4, 3, 1, 2.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q84
items.stem: In the Literature of Romanticism there was a widespread frustration with visions experienced in dreams, in nightmares and other altered states. The following list contains poems which illustrate this theme, with one exception. Identify the exception
options: Confessions of an English Opium Eater
items.explanation: As per the official UGC answer key, Samuel Taylor Coleridge's 'Kubla Khan' (1816) is identified as the exception because its dream vision celebrates the ecstatic, godlike power of poetic creation ('a miracle of rare device'), whereas works like De Quincey's Confessions and Keats's The Fall of Hyperion emphasize anguished, nightmare visions.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q85
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. A room called earth
B. tomorrow, and tomorrow and tomorrow
C. a time to dance
D. almond: a novel
I. Sohn Won-pyung
II. Padma Venkatraman
III. Madeleine Ryan
IV. Gabrielle Zevin
items.explanation: Madeleine Ryan wrote A Room Called Earth (2020, A-III), Gabrielle Zevin authored Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow (2022, B-IV), Padma Venkatraman wrote A Time to Dance (2014, C-II), and Sohn Won-pyung wrote Almond: A Novel (2017, D-I).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q86
items.stem: His cooks with long disuse their trade forgot; Cool was his kitchen, though his brains were hot. Who is this character whose stinginess passed into a proverb ?
items.explanation: In John Dryden's political satire Absalom and Achitophel (1681), these lines describe 'Shimei' (lines 620–621), the biblical persona representing Slingsby Bethel, the fanatically republican Whig Sheriff of London who was notorious for his extreme parsimony and stingy kitchen.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q87
items.stem:
Match the following :
I. Alice Walker — 1. Invisible Man
II. Ralph Ellison — 2. The Color Purple
III. Richard Wright — 3. Their Eyes Were Watching God
IV. Zora Neale Hurston — 4. Native Son
The correct combination according to the code is :
Codes : I II III IV
items.explanation: Alice Walker wrote The Color Purple (I-2) and Ralph Ellison wrote Invisible Man (II-1), which uniquely identifies option (A) in the official UGC key (despite the printed table swapping III and IV between Richard Wright's Native Son and Zora Neale Hurston's Their Eyes Were Watching God).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q88
items.stem: Brother to a Prince and fellow to a beggar if he be found worthy. This is the epigraph to
options: Rudyard Kipling's "The Man Who Would be the King"
items.explanation: 'Brother to a Prince and fellow to a beggar if he be found worthy' is the Masonic-inspired epigraph to Rudyard Kipling's novella 'The Man Who Would Be King' (1888), which recounts the doomed imperial adventure of two British ex-soldiers, Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan, in Kafiristan.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q89
items.stem:
Match the critics and their works :
Critics / Works
(a) Edward Said / (i) The Illusions of Postmodernism
(b) Terry Eagleton / (ii) Contemporary Marxist Criticism
(c) Francis Mulhern / (iii) Theory into Practice
(d) K. M. Newton / (iv) Culture and Imperialism
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: Said wrote Culture and Imperialism, Eagleton wrote The Illusions of Postmodernism, Mulhern wrote Contemporary Marxist Criticism and Newton wrote Theory into Practice.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q90
items.stem:
Match the following :
List – I (Novels) — List – II (Last lines)
i. Lord Jim — 1. 'It was done; it was finished. Yes, she thought, laying down her brush in extreme fatigue, I have had my vision.'
ii. To the Lighthouse — 2. 'April 27. Old father, old artificer, stand me now and ever in good stead...'
iii. A Passage to India — 3. 'He feels it himself and says often that he is "preparing to leave all this; preparing to leave,…" while he waves his hands sadly at his butterflies.'
iv. A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man — 4. '"No not yet," and the sky said, "No, not there".'
Codes : i ii iii iv
items.explanation: The concluding lines match their novels as follows: Joseph Conrad's Lord Jim ends with Stein waving his hands sadly at his butterflies (i-3); Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse ends with Lily Briscoe thinking 'I have had my vision' (ii-1); E.M. Forster's A Passage to India ends with '"No, not yet," and the sky said, "No, not there"' (iii-4); and James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man ends with Stephen's diary entry of April 27 invoking 'Old father, old artificer' (iv-2).

items.title: Mock #02 · Q91
items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Drama Extract]
Read the following extract carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"From thee, even from thy virtue!
What's this, what's this? Is this her fault or mine?
The tempter or the tempted, who sins most?
Ha! Not she; nor doth she tempt: but it is I
That, lying by the violet in the sun,
Do as the carrion does, not as the flower,
Corrupt with virtuous season. Can it be
That modesty may more betray our sense
Than woman's lightness? Having waste ground enough,
Shall we desire to raze the sanctuary
And pitch our evils there? O, fie, fie, fie!
What dost thou, or what art thou, Angelo?
Dost thou desire her foully for those things
That make her good? O, let her brother live:
Thieves for their robbery have authority
When judges steal themselves. What, do I love her,
That I desire to hear her speak again,
And feast upon her eyes? What is't I dream on?
O cunning enemy, that, to catch a saint,
With saints dost bait thy hook!"
— William Shakespeare, Measure for Measure (Act II, Scene 2)

Question:
“Thieves for their robbery have authority / When judges steal themselves” implies what?
items.explanation: Angelo admits that judicial condemnation of petty criminals is hypocritical when the judges themselves commit moral robbery, as a corrupt magistrate possesses no ethical authority to condemn others.

items.title: Mock #02 · Q96
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Prose Passage]
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"Painting, or art generally, as such, with all its technicalities, difficulties, and particular ends, is nothing but a noble and expressive language, invaluable as the vehicle of thought, but by itself nothing. He who has learned what is commonly considered the whole art of painting, that is, the art of representing any natural object faithfully, has as yet only learned the language by which his thoughts are to be expressed. He has done just as much toward being that which we ought to respect as a great painter, as a man, who had learned how to express himself grammatically and melodiously, would have done toward being a great poet. The language is, indeed, more difficult of acquirement in the one case than in the other, and possesses more of intrinsic beauty; but it is, nevertheless, a language only, both being capable of deep expression, but neither of them, by itself, giving any value to the conception it conveys."
— John Ruskin, Modern Painters (Volume I)

What implicit assumption about language and expression underpins the passage’s argument?

Expression without technical skill is more valuable.
The medium of expression is secondary to the message conveyed.
The value of grammar and melody lies in their aesthetic, not communicative power
